Canard

kuh-NARD · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Canard is an unfounded rumor or story; a lie repeated as if true.

The rumor that the school was closing for good turned out to be nothing more than a canard started by a disgruntled parent online.

Worked Example

The story that eating late at night causes weight gain by itself has been repeated for decades, but nutritionists have shown it's really just a canard -- what matters is overall calories, not the clock.

A claim that gets repeated so often people assume it's true, even though it isn't, is exactly what a canard is.

Antonyms

fact

How Strong Is It? — rumor → canard → hoax

rumor vs. canard

rumor vs. canard: A rumor about the closure spread quickly, though nobody could say where it started.

hoax vs. canard

hoax vs. canard: A hoax is stronger than a canard: a canard is a false story passed along as true, while a hoax goes further -- an elaborate, staged deception complete with fake press releases and photographs.

Build the Word

The pieces

origin — canard

origin — canard: duck (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Canard is simply the French word for 'duck.' The false-story meaning is thought to come from an old French idiom about half-selling a duck -- an old expression for fooling someone -- and the word crossed into English still carrying that sense of a fabricated tale.

Use the root in a new word: duck

Strength Check

Word Choice

Canard is a somewhat formal, almost journalistic word for a persistent false story -- it works well for a repeated myth or rumor, but sounds odd for a single small lie.
